extracted.intended_audience: policy scholars, regulators, advocacy groups, and practitioners interested in administrative rulemaking and notice-and-comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how organized collections of identical or near-duplicate public comments (mass comment campaigns) affect agency rulemaking outcomes, including how agencies respond and whether rule content changes. The paper empirically analyzes over 1,000 EPA campaigns from 2012–2016 to measure procedural and substantive responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comment campaigns elicit a limited degree of procedural responsiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper finds that procedurally the vast majority of mass comment campaigns receive responses from the agency. Procedural responsiveness refers to whether agencies engage with or acknowledge campaigns in the rulemaking record (e.g., by responding in rule preambles or docket materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comment campaigns do not elicit substantive responsiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive responsiveness refers to whether the content of rules is consistent with or changed in response to the campaigns' substantive demands. The analysis demonstrates little consistency between mass comment campaigns and the content of rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of agency response
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner in which the agency responds to campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study addresses how agencies respond (e.g., acknowledgement, summary, engagement with arguments, form-letter replies). While the abstract does not detail response types, it highlights that the analysis explicitly examines the manner of agency responses to campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association between campaigns and rule substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The association between campaigns and the substance of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric assesses whether there is an observable relationship between the existence/content of mass comment campaigns and subsequent substantive provisions or language in final rules. The paper finds little consistency, suggesting weak or no substantive association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on participatory democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether mass comment campaigns enhance participatory democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper evaluates if campaigns meaningfully improve public participation or democratic engagement in rulemaking. The findings suggest that campaigns have neither enhanced participatory democracy nor produced substantive democratic benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of transforming rulemaking into 'notice and spam'
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether mass comment campaigns transform rulemaking into a process of 'notice and spam.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assesses the concern that mass, identical comments could degrade the informational quality of notice-and-comment processes. The authors conclude campaigns did not transform rulemaking into 'notice and spam' in their study period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical scope / dataset coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a comprehensive empirical dataset (information about more than 1,000 mass comment campaigns during EPA rulemakings between 2012 and 2016) to evaluate efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study's conclusions are grounded in assembling and analyzing over 1,000 campaigns; this metric relates to the robustness and representativeness of the evidence base (coverage across rules, campaign types, and time period) used to judge efficacy.
